original_title: Sony Awarded a Hacker $50,000 for Privately Reporting a PS5 Exploit He Found With AI — Now He's Public Enemy Number One
summary_en: A hacker known as Jordy has reportedly received a $50,000 bounty from Sony for discovering a critical PS5 exploit. This payout has stirred controversy within the PlayStation homebrew community, as the exploit was initially held back by another security researcher.
ai_analysis: The increasing sophistication of AI in uncovering complex software vulnerabilities like the PS5's hypervisor bug highlights a new arms race between console manufacturers and security researchers, impacting the future of console modding.

en.title: AI-Found PS5 Exploit Nets Hacker $50K, Ignites Homebrew Uproar
en.summary: A hacker known as Jordy has reportedly received a $50,000 bounty from Sony for discovering a critical PS5 exploit. This payout has stirred controversy within the PlayStation homebrew community, as the exploit was initially held back by another security researcher.
en.body:
The PlayStation 5 homebrew scene is abuzz with controversy following reports that a hacker, operating under the handle **Jordy**, was awarded a substantial $50,000 bounty by Sony for privately reporting a critical exploit. This exploit, which affects PS5 firmware versions from 13.60 up to 14.00, is a ‘Hypervisor Bug’. Such vulnerabilities exist within the core software layer and can allow for the execution of unauthorized code, potentially enabling users to run custom operating systems like Linux on the console.

The situation escalated because the exploit was reportedly discovered months ago by a prominent security engineer, identified as **Andy Nguyen** (aka theflow0), who had been working on bringing Linux to the PS5 since March. Nguyen had apparently intended to hold onto the vulnerability until the launch of *Grand Theft Auto 6*, a decision that has now been overshadowed by Jordy's AI-assisted discovery and subsequent report to Sony via HackerOne, a platform that facilitates bug bounty programs. Sony's policy is to reward hackers for disclosing vulnerabilities and to pay them not to release this information until the security holes are patched.

## The AI Factor and Community Fallout

The role of artificial intelligence in discovering this exploit is particularly noteworthy. This incident is part of a broader trend where AI tools are accelerating the pace at which security vulnerabilities are found across the internet. Security experts have even dubbed the current period 'Black October' due to a surge in major security incidents and disclosures influenced by AI research. For the PS5 homebrew community, this development is a significant blow. The ability to run custom software on consoles has always been a driving force for enthusiasts, offering possibilities beyond official offerings. However, when such powerful exploits are monetized privately rather than shared openly, it can lead to frustration and a sense of lost opportunity for the wider community.

> "I am stepping away from the PS5 scene and stopping all my w"

This quote, attributed to theflow0, suggests a personal decision to disengage from the PS5 security research community, likely stemming from the events surrounding Jordy's bounty. The implication is that the discovery and subsequent reward have dampened the enthusiasm for continued work in this area for some key figures.

## What's Next for PS5 Security

With Sony actively rewarding private disclosures, the landscape for PS5 homebrew development remains challenging. The company’s commitment to security through its bug bounty program means that significant vulnerabilities are likely to be patched quickly, making it harder for the community to maintain access to custom firmware or unofficial software. Fans eager for new homebrew possibilities will be watching closely to see if future exploits emerge and how the community responds, especially as AI continues to evolve its capabilities in cybersecurity.

content_raw: A hacker sparked an uproar within the PlayStation 5 homebrew scene for privately reporting an exploit to Sony and cashing in on a $50,000 reward, rather than keeping it confidential for the community. A hacker who goes by the handle “Jordy” was awarded the bounty from Sony for reporting a vulnerability — found using AI — on the PS5 console. The bug was reported to HackerOne, a site that works with companies to plug issues in their products and services. Essentially, Sony pays hackers to find exploits, then pays them money not to release them until the security hole has been patched. There wouldn’t normally be anything particularly unusual about a hack being reported to Sony — but in the case of this PS5 exploit, a prominent security engineer discovered it months ago but wanted to hold onto it until GTA 6 launched. Then Jordy discovered it with AI and reported it, triggering the controversy. The exploit in question is a ‘Hypervisor Bug’ that affects the PS5 on firmware from 13.60 up to 14.00. A hypervisor bug is a fault inside the core software or firmware layer, which allows hackers to execute kernel code to, for example, boot Linux on a machine not designed to do it. You might have seen a spate of headlines about how AI has fueled an explosion of hacks across the internet. Information security experts are calling this month ‘Black October’ due to several major security incidents and vulnerability disclosures prompted by the growing use of artificial intelligence in research. Google security engineer Andy Nguyen, aka theflow0, had been working on getting Linux running on PS5 for months. Indeed, back in March, theflow0 showcased the results of his work. But Jordy’s AI-powered bug report put an end to that work. “I am stepping away from the PS5 scene and stopping all my work on PS5 Linux,” he said. “After pouring my heart and months of my life into it, including plans to finish PS5 Pro support and release in 2027, it's all down the sink. “The scene used to be a group of highly talented researchers, but now it is just a bunch of noobs using LLMs and writing hacks they don't even understand. Slop kiddies found the only hypervisor bug left, which I had also found a while ago, and decided to report to Sony.” In a conversation with IGN, Jordy admitted using generative AI to find the bug that netted him $50,000. He claimed that theflow0 found the bug back in 2025 but had kept it secret. When Jordy announced he’d found a hypervisor bug himself, theflow0 reached out to see if it was the same one he found the year before. Jordy and theflow0 initially agreed to not report the bug to HackerOne, but another researcher quickly found the same bug shortly after. Jordy made the decision to report the bug as other researchers stumbled on it by using generative AI, closing the window to claim the bounty from Sony. “I decided I would report it,” Jordy said. “If I and another person can find it with LLM, so can someone else.” theflow0 couldn’t be reached for comment.
